choices: True
False — feasible only means it satisfies the constraints
checkpoints.explanation: Feasible just means all constraints hold. Optimal is the stronger property: feasible and no feasible point has better cost. Keeping these separate is essential vocabulary.
checkpoints.question: True or false: a feasible solution must minimize the objective function.

choices: Decision variables
An objective to optimize
Constraints on the decisions
A guarantee that the optimal solution is unique
checkpoints.explanation: A mathematical program supplies variables, an objective, and constraints — but nothing promises the optimum is unique or even exists. Ties and unbounded problems are both possible.
checkpoints.question: Every mathematical program has three ingredients. Which of these is NOT one of them?

choices: Always equal to the integer program's optimal value
At least as good — an optimistic bound on it
Always strictly worse
Unrelated to the integer program's value
checkpoints.explanation: Relaxing constraints can only enlarge the feasible set, so the relaxed optimum is at least as good as the original's — an optimistic bound. It may be fractional and strictly better.
checkpoints.question: Take an integer program and relax (drop) the integrality requirement. The optimal value of the resulting LP is…

choices: Proportionality
Additivity
Divisibility
Certainty
checkpoints.explanation: You cannot buy 3.7 trucks. The decision is inherently whole-numbered, which breaks divisibility and turns the model into an integer program.
checkpoints.question: Your model has a variable x = number of delivery trucks to purchase. Which LP axiom is at risk?

choices: The 200 labor hours available
The number of units of product A to make
The $40 profit per unit of A
The number of constraints
checkpoints.explanation: The 200 hours, the $40 profit, and the constraint count are fixed data. Decision variables are the quantities of products to make.
checkpoints.question: In the production-planning LP, which of these is a decision variable?

choices: It gives fewer variables
The 5-consecutive-days rule can't be captured with y_j
y_j would have to be fractional
The objective would become nonlinear
checkpoints.explanation: With y_j = nurses working day j, there is no way to write 'each nurse works 5 consecutive days' linearly. Choosing x_j = nurses starting on day j bakes the rule into the model. Variable choice is a design decision!
checkpoints.question: In the nurse-scheduling model, why did we use x_j = nurses starting their week on day j, instead of y_j = nurses working on day j?

choices: A linear program
A mixed-integer program
A nonlinear program
Not an optimization problem
checkpoints.explanation: Whole trucks are a discrete decision, so this is a mixed-integer program. Dropping the whole-number requirement produces its LP relaxation.
checkpoints.question: A city must buy delivery trucks — whole trucks only — to serve routes at minimum cost. Which flavor of optimization is that?

choices: One ≥ constraint
Two opposing inequality constraints
A single slack variable
Nothing — equalities can't be converted
checkpoints.explanation: An equality is exactly the intersection of the two opposing inequalities: a'x = b if and only if a'x ≥ b and a'x ≤ b.
checkpoints.question: An equality constraint a'x = b can be replaced by…

choices: If n² is odd, then n is odd
If n² is even, then n is even
If n is even, then n² is even
If n² is odd, then n is even
checkpoints.explanation: For P ⇒ Q with P = 'n odd', Q = 'n² odd': the contrapositive is ¬Q ⇒ ¬P, i.e. 'if n² is even, then n is even'.
checkpoints.question: Claim: if n is odd, then n² is odd. Which statement is its contrapositive?

choices: It is true
Nothing conclusive — it remains unproven
It is false for some larger n
Induction now finishes the proof automatically
checkpoints.explanation: A million confirmations are evidence, not proof — remember n² + n + 41 surviving 39 checks. Until there's a proof, the honest status is 'open'.
checkpoints.question: A conjecture has been verified by computer for n = 1 up to 10⁶. What do we know?

choices: Direct proof
Induction
Contradiction
Counterexample
checkpoints.explanation: There's nothing to construct — you rule the object out. Assume a smallest positive rational q exists; then q/2 is a smaller one. Contradiction.
checkpoints.question: Which technique fits best: “there is no smallest positive rational number”?

lectures.description: Logical implication, proof techniques, counterexamples, mathematical writing, and a practical introduction to LaTeX.
lectures.title: Proof Techniques & LaTeX

choices: A halfspace {x: a'x ≥ b}
A line segment
A five-pointed star
The intersection of two convex sets
checkpoints.explanation: A star has 'dents': pick two points on different arms and the segment leaves the set. Halfspaces, segments, and intersections of convex sets are always convex — that last fact is exactly why polyhedra are convex.
checkpoints.question: Which of these sets is NOT convex?

choices: Show every pair y, z ∈ P has x between them
Exhibit some y, z ∈ P ∖ {x} and λ ∈ [0, 1] with x = λy + (1 − λ)z
Show x is not optimal for any cost vector
Show fewer than n constraints exist
checkpoints.explanation: Not extreme means the definition fails: there EXIST y, z in P (both ≠ x) with x on the segment between them — you must exhibit them. Getting the negation right is half the proof.
checkpoints.question: To prove x ∈ P is not an extreme point, you must…

choices: m · n
2ᵐ
C(m, n)
It can be infinite
checkpoints.explanation: The bound is (m choose n): a basic solution needs n linearly independent active constraints chosen from the m available, and each such choice pins down at most one point.
checkpoints.question: With m constraints in ℝⁿ, the number of basic solutions is at most…

lectures.description: Convexity, polyhedra, extreme points, vertices, basic feasible solutions, and adjacency.
lectures.title: The Geometry of Linear Programming I

choices: Exactly 3 components are zero
More than 3 components are zero
The basis matrix is singular
Some component is negative
checkpoints.explanation: In standard form, nonbasic variables (n − m of them) are zero by construction. Degeneracy means MORE than n − m zeros — some basic variable is zero too. Here n − m = 7 − 4 = 3.
checkpoints.question: Standard form, n = 7 variables, m = 4 equations. A basic solution is degenerate when…

choices: The unit square
A halfplane in ℝ²
A triangle
A nonempty standard-form polyhedron
checkpoints.explanation: A halfplane contains lines, so it has no extreme point (Thm 2.6). The square and triangle are polytopes; standard-form polyhedra always have a BFS by Corollary 2.2.
checkpoints.question: Which polyhedron has no extreme point?

choices: Every optimal solution is an extreme point
At least one optimal solution is an extreme point
The optimal solution is unique
P is bounded
checkpoints.explanation: Thm 2.7 says SOME optimal solution is at an extreme point — others may exist (a whole optimal edge, say). It does not force uniqueness or boundedness.
checkpoints.question: P has an extreme point and the LP has an optimal solution. Which is guaranteed?

lectures.description: Standard-form bases, degeneracy, existence and optimality of extreme points, convex hulls, and Fourier–Motzkin elimination.
lectures.title: The Geometry of Linear Programming II

choices: The current basis
The current dictionary
The feasible polyhedron
The current endpoint
checkpoints.explanation: A pivot changes the basis, dictionary, and usually the current endpoint. It does not change the feasible polyhedron defined by the original constraints.
checkpoints.question: What remains unchanged during a simplex pivot?

choices: The current basic feasible solution is optimal
The current basic feasible solution is unique
The feasible polyhedron is bounded
Every nonbasic variable must enter
checkpoints.explanation: Primal feasibility and nonnegative nonbasic reduced costs are the two checks for an optimal basis. They do not imply uniqueness or boundedness.
checkpoints.question: For a feasible basis in a minimization LP, what does every nonbasic reduced cost being nonnegative certify?

choices: The current basis is optimal
The ratio test chooses the largest basic direction component
The direction is blocked at step zero
The path stays feasible for every nonnegative step and the objective is unbounded below
checkpoints.explanation: No basic variable decreases, so no variable blocks the move. The direction preserves the equalities, and its negative objective slope makes the feasible ray unbounded below.
checkpoints.question: At a basic feasible solution of a minimization LP, an entering variable has negative reduced cost and d_B ≥ 0. What follows?

choices: The entering variable has zero reduced cost
The basis matrix is singular
The basic variable x₆ is already zero and would decrease, so the ratio test gives θ = 0
Every reduced cost is nonnegative
checkpoints.explanation: After the first pivot, x₆ is basic at zero. Increasing x₂ would make x₆ negative, so the maximum feasible step is zero. We can still exchange x₂ and x₆ in the basis; the dictionary changes while the point and objective stay fixed.
checkpoints.question: Why does the second pivot change the basis but leave the point and objective unchanged?

lectures.description: Basis partitions, equality-preserving feasible directions, maximum feasible steps, reduced costs, and the basis optimality test.
lectures.title: Simplex I: Basis Directions and Reduced Costs

choices: Only the objective value
The initial basis and complete tableau
Only the entering variable
A positive-length edge step
checkpoints.explanation: The sixth pivot restores the initial basis and every tableau entry. The fixed pivot rules then repeat the same six choices. The point and objective were unchanged throughout.
checkpoints.question: In Example 3.6, what repeats after the six zero-length pivots?

choices: It has the largest pivot entry
Its basic variable has the smallest index
The first unequal normalized entries satisfy 7/9 < 5/3
The row with the negative pivot entry leaves
checkpoints.explanation: Lexicographic comparison starts at column 0 and stops at the first difference. The first difference is in column 2: 7/9 is smaller than 5/3, so normalized row 3 is smaller.
checkpoints.question: In Example 3.7, the ordinary ratios and the next entries tie. What selects row 3?

choices: Most negative reduced cost; smallest-index leaving variable
Smallest eligible entering index; smallest variable index among minimum-ratio ties
Smallest row number for both choices
Smallest entering index; largest feasible ratio
checkpoints.explanation: Bland uses the smallest variable index for the entering choice and for ties in the ordinary minimum-ratio test. Choosing a leaving variable by its row position, or choosing the most negative entering cost, is a different rule.
checkpoints.question: Which pair of choices is Bland’s anticycling rule?

choices: The original LP is infeasible
The original LP is already optimal
An original feasible point exists, but its basis may still need cleanup
The artificial variable must become positive before Phase II
checkpoints.explanation: A zero sum of nonnegative artificial variables makes every artificial variable zero. The original variables are feasible. A zero artificial variable may remain in a degenerate basis, so we still need an original-variable basis and the original objective row.
checkpoints.question: Phase I ends with objective zero and an artificial variable still basic at zero. What do we know?

choices: Yes: the zero right-hand side makes this a basis change at the same feasible point
No: every pivot element must be positive
No: a negative coefficient proves infeasibility
Only if the Phase I objective increases
checkpoints.explanation: Cleanup changes the basis without taking a positive step. Dividing a zero-right-hand-side row by a negative pivot still leaves its right-hand side zero; eliminating that column from other rows does not change their right-hand sides. The feasible point is preserved.
checkpoints.question: An artificial basic variable has value zero. Its tableau row contains a negative, nonzero coefficient in an original column. Can we pivot on it?

choices: The feasible set has changed
The basis columns must always become artificial again
A zero Phase I cost means every original reduced cost is zero
Phase I minimized artificial variables; Phase II uses the original cost vector
checkpoints.explanation: The constraint rows keep the feasible basis, but reduced costs depend on the objective. Recompute the current cost and every reduced cost using the original coefficients. Example 3.8 changes from Phase I cost zero to original cost 11/6 with a negative reduced cost for x4.
checkpoints.question: After all artificial columns are removed, why must we recompute the objective row?

choices: It is a negative reduced cost; a feasible positive step lowers the objective.
It gives the maximum feasible step.
It identifies the leaving basic point without a ratio test.
It proves that the original LP is infeasible.
checkpoints.explanation: The signed height difference is the reduced cost. It gives the objective slope. Feasibility and the ratio test still decide whether a positive step is possible and which variable leaves.
checkpoints.question: A nonbasic lifted point is below the current dual plane. What does its signed vertical gap tell us?

choices: All eight points are basic.
The requirement line can no longer meet the convex hull.
Every convex combination lies on or above that line, so no feasible mixture at b can have lower cost.
Every feasible mixture must use exactly the same weights.
checkpoints.explanation: A supporting line bounds the cost of every convex combination from below. At the required horizontal coordinate, the mixture of points 5 and 8 attains the bound. Other optimal mixtures could exist in a different example.
checkpoints.question: In the final basis 5, 8, every lifted point is on or above the line through 5 and 8. Why is the current feasible mixture optimal?

choices: Every pivoting rule needs exponentially many pivots
Some pivoting rule can follow an exponentially long improving path
Simplex can never solve a cube quickly
Avoiding cycling guarantees a short path
checkpoints.explanation: The construction supplies a long improving path and a rule that follows it. The same starting and optimal vertices are adjacent, allowing another rule to finish in one pivot.
checkpoints.question: What does the perturbed-cube example establish?

choices: Diameter counts Euclidean distance
A short graph path need not be improving or efficiently found by the pivot rule
Polyhedra have no vertex graphs
Polynomial diameter implies every path is short
checkpoints.explanation: Diameter bounds the shortest unrestricted edge paths. A chosen simplex rule follows improving feasible pivots, and may also take degenerate zero steps; neither behavior is bounded by diameter alone.
checkpoints.question: Why would a polynomial diameter bound alone be insufficient to prove simplex runs in polynomial time?
